value.overview: The Anhinga is a long-necked waterbird of the warmer parts of the Americas. It is often called a snakebird because it swims with only its slender neck and head above the surface. Unlike many waterbirds, its feathers are not highly waterproof, allowing it to dive efficiently but requiring frequent wing-spreading to dry. Anhingas hunt mainly by swimming underwater and stabbing fish with their sharp, pointed bills.
value.classification: The Anhinga belongs to the order Suliformes and family Anhingidae. Its scientific name is Anhinga anhinga.
value.identification: Anhingas are large, slim waterbirds with very long necks, pointed bills, broad wings, and long tails. Adult males are mostly glossy black, with striking silvery-white markings on the wings and back. Females and immature birds have brown bodies and paler brown heads and necks. The species can be distinguished from cormorants by its sharply pointed bill, longer neck and tail, and habit of swimming low in the water. It often perches with its wings spread to dry.
value.rangeHabitat: The Anhinga occurs from the southern United States through Mexico and Central America to much of South America and the Caribbean. In Costa Rica it is a widespread but generally uncommon resident of the lowlands on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes. It uses freshwater lakes, slow rivers, marshes, lagoons, ponds, reservoirs, mangroves, and quiet coastal wetlands. Important Costa Rican areas include the Tempisque and Bebedero lowlands, Río Frío, and Caño Negro, where suitable nesting and feeding wetlands support higher numbers.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Anhinga is considered primarily resident and can occur throughout the year. Northern populations are partly migratory, but individuals in Costa Rica generally do not undertake regular long-distance seasonal movements. Local movements may occur when water levels, prey availability, or wetland conditions change.
value.breeding: Anhingas usually nest in trees or shrubs standing near or over water, sometimes alone and sometimes in small mixed colonies with other waterbirds. The nest is a shallow platform made from sticks and leafy material. A typical clutch contains about three to five pale bluish or greenish eggs. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly in lowland wetlands, with nesting activity extending through much of the year and often increasing during the wetter months.
value.dietFeeding: The Anhinga feeds chiefly on fish, but it also takes aquatic insects, crustaceans, amphibians, and occasionally other small aquatic animals. It hunts by diving and swimming underwater, using its powerful feet for propulsion and its pointed bill to spear or seize prey. After feeding, it commonly rests on exposed branches, snags, or mangrove limbs, where it spreads its wings to dry.
value.behavior: Anhingas are strong swimmers and divers but are less buoyant than ducks because their feathers become waterlogged. They may swim with only the head and neck visible, then dive suddenly when approaching prey. They are often seen singly or in small groups, although larger gatherings may form near productive wetlands or nesting sites. Their long necks may be held in an S-shape, and they sometimes soar on rising air currents.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable to increasing, although local numbers may vary with wetland conditions and habitat quality.
